item.description: barefoot. “Coiseachd caisig”.
applied to someone who was retentive regarding the way of life of the area prior to his own birth. “Bha sean chluas ormsa.”
informant uses this to mean your chest. Cited example of a horse stuck in a bog, being submerged completely up to his chest – “suas gu sgoilteadh”.
applied to someone who is always busy.
a rock upon which you would have a rest, breather.
a short while.
doing something in a hurry.
a medical check up.
a cap with a polished bill made of shiny, plastic material. Worn by old fishermen. Similar to a postman’s cap.
the milt of a female herring.
this is said when a job is near completion.
applied to a person who is always changing occupations. Also used in the sense of changeable weather conditions.
similarly [cf. ath sgeimail] used of a person changing jobs frequently.
minnows.
artistic design on the front of a shoe.
the uppers of a shoe.
the nest in a fireplace.
“A cheud Di Mairt de sholus an earraich” – Shrove Tuesday.
this is used to indicate a short account of a certain topic. “Thug e teacs air a’ bhainnis.”
to give a report on a subject.
“Bha i an aois sin aig an obair sin.” ‘Aois’ used in the sense of a person being in a job for a number of years.
damned, e.g. “duine damainte”.
“Ghabh sinn deagh shearrag.” – to have consumed a fair amount of drink.
when some commodity has been wasted, e.g. when food has gone past its sell by date.
applied to a two-faced person.
the traveller on boat used to hoist the sail.
halyard.
ropes, e.g. “Bha sia fodhlaichean air a bhàta.”
a breeze of wind. “Bha éarrag gaoithe ann.”
long jump.
a limp. “Bha beic ann.”
a male goose.
a chilly, nippy kind of day.
a difficult, obstinate man who is easy to incite.
anger, fury. “Bha e furasda réidse a chuir air.”
regular bouts of drinking. “Bhiodh e a gabhail gleadhagan deoch tric.”
this would be said of someone who had returned after failing to achieve what he had set out to do. “Thill e dhachaidh ’s cùl caise ri grodaig.”
mist and snow supported by a strong wind.
a strong wind.
a quiet moment, e.g. a thief waiting for a quiet moment – “Bha e a feitheamh ris an t-iomradh balbh.”
a miser.
applied to a conceited person who thought a lot of himself. “’S ann a tha rar spars.”
under strict supervision.

going back to a time when money was not so available this refers to a wedding dress which could be borrowed within a community. Following verse associated with this practice. “Cuir dhachaidh e, cuir dhachaidh e an gùn iasaid, Cuir dhachaidh e, cuir dhachaidh e mu’n tig teachdaire ga iarraidh.”
cravat.
catalogue.
a comical, jocular person.

item.description: proverb.
wide open.
an illness, disease. “Bha gaoid air.”
state, situation. “An t-omhnadh anns an robh an duine.”
sleeve coverings that reached up to your elbows. Used by cooks.
a report.
respect. “Cha d’fhuair e fiu’s raspeic.”
a dresser.
same as ‘crann deilbh’.
same as ‘crois liaghraidh’.
“Feuch nach caill thu iuchraichean do chloinne.” – said to a woman if she endangered or put herself at risk by lifting a heavy object.
would be said if your were experiencing dizziness, e.g. “Tha mo cheann na cheò bhith.”
